_about: SAMPLE OUTPUT. Written during development on 2026-11-24 with Claude Fable 5.2, by reading the Crossref abstracts in demo-sources.json. It is not the result of a live AI call inside TRACE. It has the same shape as a model answer and is loaded through the same validator (validateDraft), so every excerpt is checked against the stored abstract exactly as live output would be.
label: Sample brief (written during development, not a live AI call)

claims.text: Students who took practice recall tests remembered more of a prose passage on tests two days and one week later than students who restudied it, although restudying gave better recall after five minutes.
claims.excerpt: When the final test was given after 5 min, repeated studying improved recall relative to repeated testing. However, on the delayed tests, prior testing produced substantially greater retention than studying
claims.limitations: Abstract only. It reports two experiments with prose passages and gives no effect sizes.

claims.text: Once an item had been learned, studying it again did not improve delayed recall, whereas being tested on it again did.
claims.excerpt: Repeated studying after learning had no effect on delayed recall, but repeated testing produced a large positive effect.
claims.limitations: Abstract only. The material was foreign language vocabulary, so the result may not carry over to other kinds of learning.

claims.text: A meta-analysis found practice tests more beneficial for learning than restudying.
claims.excerpt: Results reveal that practice tests are more beneficial for learning than restudying and all other comparison conditions.
claims.limitations: Abstract only. No effect sizes are quoted, and the abstract says the effect varied with features of the tests, participants and studies.

claims.text: A review of ten learning techniques recommended practice testing in place of rereading, which it found does not consistently improve performance.
claims.excerpt: Most students report rereading and highlighting, yet these techniques do not consistently boost students’ performance, so other techniques should be used in their place (e.g., practice testing instead of rereading).
claims.limitations: Abstract only. The abstract summarises a long monograph and does not show how each rating was reached.

claims.text: Taken together, this suggests that when the goal is to remember material for more than a few days, some rereading time is better spent on self-testing.
claims.limitations: This is a synthesis across the passages above. No single passage states it.
